problem: Earlier language-grounding benchmarks miss the complexity of real household instruction following. R2R and Touchdown are navigation-only on static graphs. EQA and IQA use templated language. VirtualHome lacks egocentric feedback and partial observability. VSP and CHAI select objects by class or a generic 'interact' action. None combines long-horizon, compositional tasks with irreversible state changes and pixel-level object interaction driven by free-form human language.
motivation: Robots in homes need to map task-oriented language like 'Rinse off a mug and place it in the coffee maker' to long sequences of navigation and manipulation under partial observability, where some actions (slicing, heating) cannot be undone. VLN progress (Seq2Seq, progress monitors, beam search, backtracking) may not transfer: beam search and backtracking are infeasible when actions are irreversible and horizons average about 50 steps, so a harder benchmark is needed to expose this gap.
key_idea: ALFRED is a benchmark of 25,743 crowd-sourced high-level goals plus step-by-step instructions, paired with 8,055 PDDL-planner expert demonstrations in 120 AI2-THOR scenes, where agents must output discrete navigation and interaction actions together with pixelwise interaction masks to complete 7 compositional household task types.
insight: A VLN-style Seq2Seq model with progress monitoring, strong on navigation benchmarks, almost completely fails on ALFRED: task success is ≤4% seen and ≤0.5% unseen, and no-language and no-vision ablations still reach about 6% goal-condition success. The ablations yield three findings. Instructions-only ≈ full model, so the model ignores the high-level goal for planning. Progress monitors help only marginally, mostly on path-weighted scores. Sub-goal evaluation (Table 4) shows that object-agnostic sub-goals are easy (Cool/Heat ≈85-94%), while visual semantic navigation and mask grounding are the bottleneck, especially in unseen scenes (Goto 22, Pickup 21, Slice 12). The authors conclude that hierarchical/modular models and pretrained segmentation are the likely way forward, which is the direction later ALFRED work took.
method: Expert demonstration generation: task tuples (task type, scene, object, receptacle, secondary object) are sampled greedily to reduce imbalance. Agent and object states are encoded as PDDL rules and solved with the FF planner using full-state metadata (unavailable at test time). Demos are verified by replay; 3 demos per 2,685 parameter sets gives 8,055 demos averaging 50 steps and 428,322 image-action pairs.

Language annotation: AMT workers watch sub-goal-segmented videos and write a step-by-step instruction per PDDL sub-goal plus a high-level goal (≥3 annotators per demo). A second validation HIT removes outlier directives. Splits: train 21,023; val seen 820 / unseen 821; test seen 1,533 / unseen 1,529. Unseen folds use 4 (val) and 8 (test) held-out scenes.

Seq2Seq baseline: frozen ImageNet ResNet-18 conv5 features (512×7×7) → two 1×1 convs → FC gives a 2500-d visual feature. Goal and instructions are concatenated with <SEP> and encoded by a BiLSTM (hidden 100, from scratch). Soft attention conditioned on h_{t-1} feeds an LSTM decoder (hidden 512) with input [v_t; x̂_t; a_{t-1}].

Action + mask heads: an FC layer over [h_t; u_t] predicts 13 actions (5 navigation, 7 interaction, Stop). A 3-layer deconv network outputs a 300×300 sigmoid interaction mask. Mask-to-object resolution uses IoU with simulator ground-truth object masks. Training is imitation learning with CE (action) and rebalanced BCE (mask), Adam at lr 1e-4, dropout 0.3.
Progress monitors (Seq2Seq+PM): two auxiliary sigmoid heads, each weighted 0.1 with L2 loss. One regresses normalized time t/T; the other regresses the normalized number of completed sub-goals c_t/C.

Evaluation protocol: Task Success (all goal-conditions satisfied at episode end) and Goal-Condition Success (fraction satisfied), each with path-length weighting relative to the expert. Episodes terminate after 1000 steps or 10 failed actions. A separate sub-goal evaluation teacher-forces the expert up to a sub-goal, then lets the agent complete it.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 (frozen, ImageNet-pretrained) + BiLSTM encoder + LSTM decoder with deconv mask head (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: ALFRED train split (21,023 language directives over expert PDDL demonstrations, 108 scenes); imitation learning only, no extra data
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB (300×300 saved, resized to 224×224) + natural-language goal and step-by-step instructions
setting.action_space: 13 discrete actions: MoveAhead, RotateLeft/Right, LookUp/Down, Pickup, Put, Open, Close, ToggleOn, ToggleOff, Slice, Stop; interaction actions require a pixelwise object mask
setting.privileged: none for full-task evaluation (the interaction API resolves the predicted mask to an object via IoU with simulator GT instance masks); sub-goal evaluation teacher-forces the expert trajectory up to the evaluated sub-goal

numbers_note: Split vocabulary has no 'test-seen', so the ALFRED test-seen fold is recorded as split 'test' with 'test SEEN fold' in extra. Metric keys: SR = Task Success, GC = Goal-Condition Success, PLWSR/PLWGC = path-length-weighted versions (the parenthesized values). Other rows not listed as own-method entries: No Language, No Vision, Goal-only, Instructions-only, PM Progress-only and PM SubGoal-only (Table 3); per-task-type success (Table A1); and an 'Oracle step-by-step evaluation' appendix table (All Inputs val-seen SR 3.0 (1.2), GC 10.0 (6.0)). Human performance was measured on 100 random test-unseen directives: SR 91.0 (85.8), GC 94.5 (87.6).
results: The best baseline, Seq2Seq+PM, reaches only 3.7% / 4.0% task success on val/test seen and 0.0% / 0.4% on val/test unseen, with goal-condition success of about 7-10%. Humans score 91.0% SR and 94.5% GC on 100 test-unseen directives, and a random agent scores 0%. No-language and no-vision ablations still reach about 6% goal-condition success. Progress monitors raise seen task success from about 2% to about 4% and improve path-weighted scores, but give no gain in unseen scenes.
limitations: The only baselines are a simple Seq2Seq/PM imitation model with near-zero unseen success. There is no DAgger or RL, since re-planning after irreversible actions (e.g., slicing the only apple) is non-trivial or impossible.
Navigation is discretized grid movement in synthetic AI2-THOR scenes; mask-based interaction is resolved via simulator ground-truth masks (IoU), so there is no real physical manipulation.
Checkpoints are selected by validation-seen loss, which may not correlate with task success because agents need not imitate the expert exactly.
